answer.label: Not Martin Luther — an untraced modern line
answer.authorDates: 1483–1546 · German reformer (credited, but this wording is not in his works)
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Luther, but the wording appears in none of his works. A 2005 Word & World editorial found it nowhere in the American Edition of Luther’s Works, nor, “as far as I can tell,” in the Weimar edition, and called it “apparently invented.” The only source quoters point to is a 1994 Our Daily Bread devotional, which names no work by Luther. The general idea that ordinary work pleases God does echo Luther’s real teaching on vocation.

source.excerpt: The maid who sweeps her kitchen is doing the will of God just as much as the monk who prays—not because she may sing a Christian hymn as she sweeps but because God loves clean floors. The Christian shoemaker does his Christian duty not by putting little crosses on the shoes, but by making good shoes, because God is interested in good craftsmanship.
trail: 1994: the RBC Ministries devotional Our Daily Bread for Labor Day, 5 September 1994 ↗, prints the maid and shoemaker passage as something Luther “wrote,” with no work named.
2004: Lutheran Partners editor William Decker used the quote but reported he could not trace it to Luther. He asked readers for help and got no responses, according to Word & World’s footnotes ↗.

2005: the Word & World editorial ↗ (Luther Seminary) reports that the quote does not turn up in an electronic search of the American Edition of Luther’s Works, nor, as far as the writer could tell, in the Weimar edition. It calls the quote “apparently invented.”
2014 and 2018: Justin Taylor of The Gospel Coalition lists it among the most famous things Luther never actually said ↗, relying on the Word & World critique.
source.excerptNote: The fuller two-sentence version as printed in the 1994 Our Daily Bread devotional ↗, which credits it to Luther but cites no work. The popular form usually drops the maid sentence and shortens “his Christian duty” to “his duty.”

source.rightsNote: The wording is found in none of Luther’s works, and whoever first wrote it is unknown, so no public-domain status is claimed. The only cited source, the 1994 Our Daily Bread devotional, is a modern publication. Its archived web page carries a 1996 RBC Ministries copyright notice.

author.name: Martin Luther
author.heading: About Martin Luther
author.metaLine: 1483–1546 · German priest, theologian and leader of the Protestant Reformation
author.bio: Martin Luther (10 November 1483 – 18 February 1546) was a German priest and scholar whose ideas sparked the Protestant Reformation. His teaching on vocation, that ordinary work serves God and neighbor as truly as monastic life, is real. But the polished “little crosses on the shoes” line is not found in his works.

misattribution.heading: How a modern line became “Luther”
misattribution.intro: This line circulates under Luther’s name in devotionals, sermons and quote sites. No one quoting it cites a work of Luther’s, and scholars who searched his collected works did not find it.

items.why: The 2005 Word & World editorial ↗ searched the American Edition and the Weimar edition for the quote and found nothing. It also argues that the quote’s idea, that work becomes “Christian” by adding hymns or little crosses, “seems altogether too modern” for Luther.

The Labor Day 1994 devotional ↗ introduced the passage with “Martin Luther understood this when he wrote” but gave no title, sermon or letter. Word & World found that websites citing anything for the quote cited this devotional, not a work by Luther. That does not establish the devotional as the line’s first appearance.

In the Fourth Commandment section (¶145), Luther does say a servant-girl’s housework is “better than all the sanctity and ascetic life of monks” (Triglot Concordia translation, 1921 ↗). But the passage contains nothing about clean floors, shoemakers or crosses.

misattribution.truthLine: The wording is not Luther’s. It cannot be found in his collected works, and the only source quoters point to is a 1994 devotional, as documented by Word & World 25/4 ↗. Its general theme, that ordinary work is a real calling, is genuinely Lutheran.

context.heading: Why the misquote matters
lead: Luther did teach that a farmer, a tailor or a maid serves God in daily work as truly as a monk at prayer. That is why the shoemaker line sounds right. The Word & World editorial ↗ argues that it still gets Luther wrong on the central point. The quote says work pleases God because God likes quality. That is closer to an American work ethic in which work is an end in itself. In Luther, work is done to serve the neighbor.

The editorial puts it this way: God likes good shoes “not for their own sake, but because the neighbor needs shoes.” It warns that, in the mouth of a modern boss, the invented line could become a tool to push the bottom line.
context.detailsSummary: What Luther actually said about tailors and shoemakers
detailsBody: The pull-quote above is genuine Luther: the Large Catechism, Fourth Commandment, ¶145, in the 1921 Triglot Concordia translation ↗.

As a contrast to the invented quote, Word & World offers a sermon Luther preached in the Castle Church at Weimar on 25 October 1522 (Weimar edition 10/3:382), in the editor’s own translation: “The same is true for shoemaker, tailor, scribe, or reader. If he is a Christian tailor, he will say: I make these clothes because God has bidden me do so, so that I can earn a living, so that I can help and serve my neighbor.”
context.pull: If you perform your daily domestic task, this is better than all the sanctity and ascetic life of monks.
